terms.plain: The extra money a loan pays you for waiting.
An IOU: you lend money and get paid interest for waiting.
The US central bank. It sets the country's main interest rate.
The price of borrowing money, given as a percent per year.
How fast prices rise. At 3%, things cost 3% more than last year.
The Fed's favourite measure of how fast prices are rising.
The best known measure of how fast shop prices are rising.
How fast prices are rising for producers, before they reach shops.
The share of people who want a job but do not have one.
A monthly count of how many jobs America added or lost.
Short for the monthly jobs count. It means non-farm payrolls.
The number of people on company payrolls, counted each month.
A weekly count of people newly asking for unemployment support.
A monthly count of how many job openings employers have posted.
The total value of everything a country produces in a year.
A line showing what loans pay at different lengths of time.
When short loans pay more than long ones. A recession warning light.
What a bond pays after you subtract inflation. The number gold competes with.
One hundredth of a percent. Fifty of them make half a percent.
The gap between two rates, such as long loans minus short ones.
Something people buy when they are scared, like gold or government bonds.
How willing people feel about owning risky things like shares.
The Fed creating money to buy bonds. Think of a money hose turned on.
The Fed taking money back out. The money hose turned off.
How much the Fed owns. It grows with the money hose on.
A weekly report showing what the largest traders are betting on.
The largest traders, who must report their bets once a week.
Bets on prices rising minus bets on prices falling.
Where today sits against history. The 90th means higher than 90% of the past.
Which season money is in: growth, top, slowdown, or thaw.
A stretch where the economy shrinks instead of growing.
The Fed meeting where the interest rate decision is made.
The price of insurance against stocks falling. It rises when people are scared.
How the US dollar is doing against a basket of other currencies.
A basket of 500 large US companies, used to track the whole market.
Leaning toward raising rates to fight rising prices.
Leaning toward lowering rates to protect jobs.
Already reflected in today's price, because people expected it.
A deal to buy or sell later at a price agreed today.
A jobs alarm: it fires when unemployment drifts up off its recent low.
How fast a number is changing, not just where it sits today.
How much a price jumps around.
How much spare money is sloshing around looking for a home.
How often two things move together. It is a tendency, never a rule.
